newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Leaderless, Cambodia's opposition army retreats.
newsitem.headline: Leaderless, Cambodia's opposition army retreats.

text.p: Their leader ousted in a bloody coup and many of their key generals killed, wounded or coopted, Cambodia's rag-tag opposition army is staging a desperate retreat into the country's jungles.

Soldiers loyal to deposed First Prime Minister Norodom Ranariddh are withdrawing into northwestern Cambodia along with some Khmer Rouge forces, laying mines, blowing up bridges and counting on the rainy season to delay pursuing government troops.
Outnumbered, harried by sporadic government rocket and artillery fire, the opposition army seems keen to retreat and regroup rather than stand and fight.

Government troops chased them along Route 6 through shimmering rice paddies dotted with sugar palms as far as Kralanh and Route 68 on Sunday, about 60 km (37 miles) west of Siem Reap and the Angkor Wat temple complex.
"The (Ranariddh) forces ... are now vastly overpowered," Robert Karniol, Asia-Pacific Editor for Jane's Defence Weekly, told Reuters on Monday.
"Only two of eleven divisions have declared for (Ranariddh). Most of the Khmer Rouge defectors have stood back and not declared for anyone. And the hard-core Khmer Rouge in Anlong Veng are out of it.
"Now isn't a good time for them (the opposition) to engage Hun Sen. They must buy time, get organised, look for alliances," he said.

As his soldiers tramped through the hot, humid, malarial countryside, lighting roadside fires for their meals and stringing hammocks to sleep in, Ranariddh is jetting around the world seeking diplomatic support.
He has had some success. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations has deferred Cambodia's membership and both the United States and Germany have suspended aid to his country, at least temporarily.

Ranariddh, winner of Cambodia's U.N.-sanctioned free elections in 1993, is trying to persuade the world to give him back what Second Prime Minister Hun Sen took away eight days ago -- political primacy in Phnom Penh.
Ranariddh was out of the country when heavy fighting between forces loyal to the rival co-premiers on July 5-6 left about 60 persons dead in Cambodia's capital and his troops thoroughly defeated.
Ranariddh's strongest general, Nhiek Bun Chhay, has since disappeared. Phnom Penh is abuzz with rumours the charismatic general has been wounded or captured and executed.
As Deputy Chief of Staff of the Cambodian army, Nhiek Bun Chhay commanded the loyalties of about 40 per cent of the country's troops before the coup.
He also enjoyed the respect of some recently defected divisions of the Khmer Rouge, the guerrilla remnants of a movement that reigned over Cambodia during the 1975-79 "killing fields" years.
Nhiek Bun Chhay's ties with the Khmer Rouge, his determination to better arm and equip Ranariddh's soldiers and his power in northwestern Cambodia made him an obvious target of Hun Sen's coup forces.

While Nhiek Bun Chhay's exact fate remains uncertain, there is no doubt what happened to Ranariddh loyalists General Chao Samboth and Ho Sok, secretary of state of the Interior Ministry. Both are dead, by Hun Sen's own admission.

Other military and political leaders of the FUNCINPEC political party which Ranariddh heads are being coopted by Hun Sen, who is effectively making them offers they can't refuse to remain as part of a de-fanged opposition.
The strategy could leave Hun Sen with all the real power in a government reconstituted to present a veneer of democratic legitimacy to critical foreign governments.

Thus Prince Ranariddh's top military advisor, General Tom Sambol, was trotted out for the press late last week and flown to the provincial capitals of Siem Reap and Battambang as proof of continued pluralism in Cambodia.
Sambol was clearly uncomfortable but played his part in what came off as a clumsy political charade.
"Hun Sen has won the initial military battle but that doesn't mean that he has won the political war, which is more important and now his chief concern," said Jane's Karniol.

"As for Ranariddh, it is essential that he be able to demonstrate some kind of active military resistance within Cambodia. He needs that to be credible politically. That's his biggest challenge because right now he doesn't have it."
